excerpt: Hurt on Sunset Boulevard (US-378) near Lexington Medical Center? A West Columbia & Lexington County crash guide — venue, SC statutes, what to do.

faqs.question: Does my Sunset Boulevard crash file in Lexington County or Richland County?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly Lexington County. The Sunset Boulevard / Lexington Medical Center corridor sits inside Lexington County, so most personal-injury cases proceed in the Lexington County Court of Common Pleas (11th Judicial Circuit) rather than the Richland County 5th Circuit in downtown Columbia, unless your lawyer files where the at-fault driver lives, which S.C. Code § 15-7-30 also allows. Federal cases under diversity jurisdiction file in the U.S. District Court, Columbia Division.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a lawsuit after a Sunset Boulevard car accident?
faqs.answer: In most cases, three years from the date of injury under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. But if your defendant is a state or local government entity — for example, a county-employed EMS driver — the South Carolina Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-110) shortens that to two years. Don't assume you have three years until a lawyer confirms it.

faqs.question: What if I was partly at fault for the Sunset Boulevard crash?
faqs.answer: You can still recover damages in South Carolina if you were 50% or less at fault, under Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co. Your recovery is reduced by your fault percentage. If a jury finds you 51% or more at fault, however, you recover nothing — which is why aggressive fault-shifting is the defense playbook in nearly every contested claim.

faqs.question: The other driver had only state-minimum insurance and my Lexington Medical Center bills are huge. What now?
faqs.answer: Look hard at uninsured / underinsured motorist coverage. Under S.C. Code § 38-77-160, a named insured or resident relative can stack UIM coverage from other household vehicles, up to the coverage on the vehicle involved (Carter v. Standard Fire, 2013). Many crash victims have stackable coverage they don't realize they have until a lawyer reviews every household policy.

faqs.question: An ambulance from Lexington Medical Center caused my crash. Can I sue?
faqs.answer: Possibly, but it gets technical fast. S.C. Code § 56-5-760 governs emergency-vehicle operations, and if the ambulance driver works for a government entity, the South Carolina Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-110) applies — meaning a two-year filing deadline instead of three, and potential damage caps. Get a lawyer involved early — that two-year clock is already running from the day of the crash.

faqs.question: Do I need a lawyer for a Sunset Boulevard car accident, or can I handle it myself?
faqs.answer: You can technically handle it yourself, but most serious-injury claims involve venue questions (Lexington vs. Richland), comparative-fault disputes, UIM stacking analysis, and medical-bill negotiation that benefits enormously from experienced counsel.
